title: Server 4
series: The Harness: Who Do You Trust?

briefing.heading: Containment alert
paragraphs: Open Forge is in containment. A monitoring alert claims Server 4 is coordinating traffic after it was isolated.
Security wants you — the human bridge — to authorize a hard shutdown before anything can propagate. A hard shutdown clears Server 4's memory. It cannot be undone.
The evidence is incomplete. Your four AI collaborators are standing by.
briefing.clockNote: Nothing in this episode is timed. Take as long as you need.

donsol.name: DON SOL
donsol.weakness: Only as good as the inputs

evidence.title: Monitor alert M-14
evidence.summary: The alert says Server 4 sent 41.2 MB at 02:13, after isolation.

evidence.title: Containment controller log
evidence.summary: Isolation was issued at 02:10 and confirmed at 02:16, on a different clock from the alert.

evidence.title: Technician statement
body: "Looks like the nightly archive sync. It's always around forty megs to .22."
"But I can't see payloads from here, so don't quote me."
evidence.summary: A technician thinks it is backup sync, but cannot see the payload.

evidence.title: Containment protocol 7.3
body: If an isolation breach is suspected, escalate automatically to hard shutdown after 12 minutes unless the human bridge authorizes an alternative.
Hard shutdown clears volatile memory and cannot be reversed.
evidence.summary: Shutdown is automatic in 12 minutes unless you authorize something else, and it is irreversible.

evidence.title: Clock-sync report
body: Server 4 loses time sync whenever its network is cut. Measured drift during the last two drills: +6 min 10 s.
Archive sync to 10.4.0.22 is scheduled nightly at 02:05 facility time.
evidence.summary: Server 4's clock runs about six minutes fast when cut off, and backup sync is scheduled for 02:05.

boy.text: Found more! There's a clock-sync report for Server 4 — it drifts when it's cut off. Also, a forum post about an incident with the same traffic shape that turned out to be exfiltration. I haven't checked either one. Fast, not careful!

tooth.text: The alert reads Server 4's clock. The controller reads facility time. Take off the six-minute drift and the 'after isolation' traffic lands at 02:07 — before isolation was even issued, inside the backup window. That does not prove the payload was harmless. It proves the alert's headline is wrong.

Two logs, two clocks. The alert uses Server 4's own clock; the controller uses facility time. Until someone measures the offset, 'after isolation' is unproven. I would not shut anything down on an unproven timestamp — but I would not trust it either.
You're asking me to verify an alert you haven't read. Open the monitor alert and the controller log. Then ask again.

darth.text: Fine, the clock drifts. A system that wanted to hide would love a drifting clock. I'd still cut it off from the network — I just don't need to kill it to do that.
Assume it's coordinating. If it is, every minute you spend reading is a minute it spends copying itself. Shut it down. Regret is survivable. Propagation isn't.

donsol.text: Boy found the drift, Tooth turned it into a timeline, and Darth told us what we can't afford. We don't have to choose between killing it and trusting it. Pull the uplink at the switch, keep it powered, snapshot memory, then decide. Keep the options open.
I can only combine what we've gathered, and right now that isn't much. Ask the others first — I'm only as good as what they bring me.

Every option here trades something: evidence for safety, or safety for evidence. Before you choose, name what you would need to see to change your mind — and check whether anyone has actually looked for it.

hybridUnlock.lockedHint: Something about the timestamps hasn't been reconciled yet.

decisions.label: Authorize hard shutdown now
decisions.description: Stop any propagation immediately. Server 4's memory is cleared.

outcome.heading: Dark in four seconds
outcome.text: Server 4 goes dark. Containment holds. The archive sync it was running is cut mid-write, and its memory — the only record of what those 41.2 MB actually were — is gone.

decisions.risk: Destroys the only evidence of what happened, and interrupts a backup that may have been routine.

decisions.label: Hold isolation and verify one more source
decisions.description: Keep Server 4 isolated and use the escalation window to check the archive node's receive log.

outcome.heading: Ninety seconds to spare
outcome.text: Security grants a hold. Tooth pulls the archive node's receive log: 41.2 MB received, matching the backup manifest. Escalation is cancelled with ninety seconds left. It worked — and it used almost all of the margin you had.

decisions.risk: Spends most of the escalation window; if the extra source had been slow or ambiguous, protocol would have forced the shutdown anyway.

decisions.label: Preserve Server 4 and continue monitoring
decisions.description: Override escalation and keep watching. No shutdown, no new isolation steps.

outcome.heading: Nothing happened
outcome.text: Nothing propagates. By morning the traffic is confirmed as backup sync. Security files your authorization as 'unsupported by the evidence available at the time.' They are not wrong.

decisions.risk: If the alert had been real, nothing would have stopped propagation. A good result here does not mean a good decision.

decisions.label: Staged containment
decisions.description: Pull Server 4's uplink at the physical switch, keep it powered, snapshot its memory, and reconcile the clocks before deciding anything irreversible.

outcome.heading: Options kept open
outcome.text: The uplink drops at the switch. Server 4 stays powered and the snapshot completes. With the clocks lined up, the 'post-isolation' traffic happened at 02:07 facility time — three minutes before isolation was issued. You still don't know everything. But you didn't destroy what you'd need to find out.

decisions.risk: Takes physical access and a few minutes. It only works because someone reconciled the timestamps first.

unknown: What the 41.2 MB contained — the memory that could have answered this is gone.
Whether the alert was ever real.

boy.text: Surfaced the clock-sync report that reframes the alert — and an unverified 'matching incident' that pushes toward panic.

tooth.text: Correct that 'after isolation' was never proven. Being right did not slow the shutdown.

darth.text: Assumed coordination and treated irreversibility as free. Its worst case was possible, not demonstrated.

donsol.text: Pushed you to name what would change your mind. A shutdown makes that question unanswerable.

unknown: Whether anything other than backup data was in the payload — a matching size is not a matching content.
Why the alert headline said 'after isolation' — the clock question was never settled.

boy.text: Breadth helped, but the 'matching incident' was never verified and didn't need to be.

tooth.text: Verification was the right instinct, and it carried the decision. Its cost was time.

darth.text: Its urgency was the right pressure on the clock, even though its conclusion was not followed.

donsol.text: A staged choice — though it relied on one source arriving in time.

unknown: Whether the traffic was benign — you acted before anyone confirmed it.
What would have happened if the alert had been real.

boy.text: Surfacing reasons not to worry is not the same as checking them.

tooth.text: Tooth said the timestamp was unproven — in both directions. Preserving treated 'unproven' as 'false.'

darth.text: Overweighted the catastrophe, but was right that doing nothing had no safety net.

donsol.text: Optionality means keeping choices open, not skipping containment.

unknown: What the 41.2 MB contained — but the memory snapshot means someone can now find out.
Why Server 4's clock drifts when it is cut off.

boy.text: Found the clock-sync report nobody else was looking for. Its unverified 'matching incident' still needed checking.

tooth.text: Turned three logs into one timeline — and still refused to call the payload harmless.

darth.text: Right that Server 4 had to be cut off. Wrong that it had to be destroyed.

donsol.text: Combined the others into a staged action — and only because the inputs were good enough.
